paras: The killing of Caesar Stevens was the shooting of a Black laborer by a group of armed white men in a garden at Branchville, South Carolina, on October 8, 1888. Stevens was struck nine times and died the next morning, and the three men named as the shooters were not arrested in the days that followed. Papers in South Carolina and Georgia called it a cold-blooded murder and singled out the lack of arrests.

Stevens worked for A. F. H. Dukes of Branchville. According to a Branchville special to the Charleston News and Courier, on Saturday, October 6, he got into a "difficulty" with another Black man who was driving a wagon for people from the country. Dukes quieted the two men, but white friends of the driver renewed the quarrel with Stevens and threatened to kill him before leaving town that night.

On Monday morning the men returned armed with pistols and a shotgun and found Stevens at work in Dukes's garden. They opened fire at once, shooting at him twelve or fifteen times and hitting him in nine places. The correspondent named the shooters as W. L. McFail, T. S. Crumpler and J. A. Richardson and said several others were present as accessories. A Charleston dispatch added that the men rode away afterward and made no attempt to hide their identity. Stevens died at 8 o'clock the following morning.

As of October 9 and 10 no arrests had been made, and the Charleston dispatch said no attempt to arrest the men was known. A later Orangeburg report said that the three had given bail on the day of the shooting to the Branchville town council on a charge of "shooting on the street." Sheriff Sally of Orangeburg went to Barnwell County to arrest them on a charge of killing Stevens but could not find them, though he expected them to surrender. No report of a surrender, inquest, indictment or trial was found in the coverage.

The Branchville correspondent wrote that the "universal opinion of the town" held it a cold-blooded murder whose perpetrators should be punished, and described Stevens as "quiet, inoffensive" and well thought of by both white and Black residents.

Only white papers covered the killing, and they condemned it. The News and Courier special, reprinted on October 17 in the Fairfield News and Herald and the Manning Times under the headline "A Negro Killed at Branchville," said the killing recalled "the murders perpetrated by the cowboys on the frontiers of Texas." The Atlanta Constitution ran a Charleston special on October 16 as "Shot Down by Three Men" in its "Crimes and Criminals" column, calling Stevens "an inoffensive negro" and the failure to arrest anyone "the most disgraceful part of this outrage."

The Constitution's dispatch also said the cause was unknown and "not politics," since Stevens was liked by white people. The Savannah Morning News reported the sheriff's search on October 15 without comment, in a column of South Carolina news.
The accounts differ on motive: the Branchville correspondent traced the killing to the renewed Saturday quarrel, while the Charleston dispatch said the cause was not known.

reader.title: Killing of Caesar Stevens
bases: A group of armed white men, three named and several others, returned to Branchville and shot a Black man to death in a garden after threatening to kill him; no lawful authority or posse is reported (A2, A3).

Stevens was killed by three named white men acting with several others and without any legal authority (A2, A3); the only motive reported is a quarrel the men took up on behalf of another Black man, so a pretext of justice, race or tradition is implied at most, and the Charleston report said the cause was not known (A2, A3).

The Branchville special to the News and Courier (A3, reprinted A4), the separate Charleston special (A2) and the Orangeburg sheriff item (A1) agree on the victim, the place and the three shooters' names.

accounts.label: Branchville correspondent (News and Courier)
accounts.gist: A quarrel between Stevens and a Black wagon driver on Saturday was renewed by the driver's white friends, who threatened to kill Stevens, returned armed on Monday and shot him at work in Dukes's garden.

accounts.label: Charleston special
accounts.gist: Three white men with others shot Stevens in a garden near Branchville and rode away without hiding their identity; the cause was not known and was not politics.

accounts.label: Orangeburg report
accounts.gist: The sheriff sought the three in Barnwell county on a charge of killing Stevens; they had already given bail to the town council on a street-shooting charge.

framing.detail: The Branchville special called it 'brutally murdered' and compared it to cowboy murders on the Texas frontier; reprinted as 'A Negro Killed at Branchville.'
The Atlanta Constitution ran it as 'Shot Down by Three Men' and called the absence of arrests 'the most disgraceful part of this outrage.'
The Savannah Morning News noted the sheriff's search in a column of South Carolina briefs without comment.

versions.value: A quarrel with another Black man, renewed by that man's white friends

conflicts.note: The Branchville correspondent's local account (A3) gives the fuller background; the Charleston special (A2) says only that the cause was unknown.

versions.value: No arrests and no attempt to arrest
The three gave bail to the town council the same day on a street-shooting charge; the sheriff later sought them for the killing

conflicts.note: A1 is later and from Orangeburg; the bail was on a lesser town charge, so the reports may both be accurate.
